publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining classroom IoT pilots, machine-learning occupancy inference, edge vision counting, BAS-integrated monitoring, and official school IAQ guidance.
country_and_climate: The evidence spans university and school settings in Indonesia, Portugal, Slovenia, Romania, and general U.S. school guidance. The climates and building operations differ, but the common pattern is that occupancy-driven indoor conditions are highly sensitive to schedule, ventilation mode, and whether rooms are naturally ventilated, mixed-mode, or mechanically conditioned.
objective_and_research_question: The central objective is to understand how occupancy density, schedules, transitions between classes, and user activity shape classroom environmental conditions and how those contextual variables should be measured in an IoT monitoring system. The practical research question is not only whether a room is occupied, but whether the system can distinguish presence, approximate people count, and capture activity context well enough to explain CO2, temperature, humidity, and perceived air-quality patterns and to trigger useful operational decisions.
study_design: The evidence base is mixed: real-world classroom pilots, observational IAQ monitoring, machine-learning occupancy estimation from environmental data, edge-AI people-counting deployments, and mixed-methods studies combining sensor streams with occupant feedback. Most studies are non-randomized field evaluations in actively used educational spaces.
educational_context: The strongest directly relevant settings are elementary-school classrooms, university classrooms, laboratories, and lecture spaces. These environments are characterized by dense but time-varying occupancy, largely sedentary activity with periodic vocal peaks, scheduled breaks, and frequent mismatch between nominal room capacity and actual classroom use.
sample_and_duration: The reviewed evidence ranges from single-classroom pilot deployments to multi-classroom school programs. A strong school-based example is the Slovenian study by Vake et al. 2025, which placed 8 air-quality sensors in elementary-school classrooms and monitored VOC, CO, temperature, and humidity for 6 months while school staff collected anonymous occupancy labels. Complementary classroom pilots in Portugal and Indonesia demonstrate shorter but operationally relevant monitoring of occupancy-linked IAQ dynamics in active teaching spaces.
environmental_variables: Occupancy-sensitive monitoring in classrooms should include explicit presence or people count when possible, plus time-stamped CO2, temperature, relative humidity, and optionally VOC or PM. The most useful contextual variables are class schedule, occupied versus unoccupied state, lesson duration, room turnover, window and door state, and whether a period involves quiet seated work, discussion, or other higher-emission activity.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor weather and baseline conditions matter even for occupancy research because they shape window opening, infiltration, and HVAC operation, which in turn determine whether the environmental signal reflects human presence or ventilation change. The Slovenian occupancy-estimation study explicitly improved inference by pairing indoor IAQ data with external weather data, illustrating that occupancy modeling should not treat indoor signals in isolation.
occupancy_and_activity: Occupancy in classrooms is not a static count. Density, duration of stay, turnover between classes, absenteeism, speaking intensity, computer use, door opening, and teacher-led versus group activity all change the magnitude and timing of heat, moisture, and CO2 emissions. Sedentary classroom use is the default assumption for many comfort standards, but real classroom use repeatedly departs from that assumption through transitions, vocal activity, and bursty periods of crowding.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Occupancy data is only operationally meaningful when interpreted alongside ventilation mode and control logic. The same headcount can produce very different CO2 and comfort outcomes depending on whether the room relies on natural ventilation, a fixed BAS schedule, demand-controlled ventilation, or manual window-opening behavior. Occupancy-aware monitoring is therefore most useful when it normalizes environmental data by how much outdoor air and air movement the room actually receives.
spatial_granularity: Room-level monitoring is the minimum defensible granularity. For environmental sensing, one well-sited node per classroom is often enough for operational screening, but explicit occupancy sensing can require different geometry: doorway counting, ceiling coverage, or wide field-of-view wall or edge devices. The 2025 KNX educational-facility study also reinforces that fixed wall-mounted nodes may under-represent local peaks and can miss spatial heterogeneity within occupied rooms.
sensor_specification: For classroom occupancy, the recommended sensing hierarchy is: privacy-preserving mmWave radar or dedicated people-counting depth/ToF systems when actual presence and count are needed; PIR when only coarse occupied or unoccupied status is required; and camera-based edge counting only when institutional privacy governance is mature and count accuracy is mission-critical. Evidence in the reviewed studies is strongest for class-level environmental sensing plus either inferred occupancy from IAQ data or vision-based people counting, rather than for one universal occupancy module or model.
calibration_and_qaqc: QA/QC should include time synchronization across occupancy and IAQ streams, manual ground-truth head counts for selected periods, validation against schedules, and testing under both low and high occupancy. For edge vision or mmWave systems, commissioning should verify field of view, occlusion zones, and false detections at doors. For inference-based occupancy models, training and validation data should be collected across multiple rooms, seasons, and timetable conditions rather than a single classroom pattern.
acquisition_and_data_quality: Second-level or sub-minute sampling is useful for explicit occupancy sensing and transitions, while 1 to 5 minute aggregation is usually enough for HVAC response and dashboards. Data quality problems include clock drift, missing labels, false transitions during short exits, sensor dropout, and mismatch between scheduled occupancy and actual attendance. The occupancy label itself often becomes the weakest part of the dataset unless ground truth is systematically recorded.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Explicit occupancy sensors are generally durable, but field reliability depends more on placement, power stability, firmware, lens cleanliness, and network uptime than on the sensing principle alone. Inference-only approaches reduce hardware burden but shift maintenance into model retraining, metadata upkeep, and periodic revalidation as room use patterns change.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For occupied or unoccupied state, a low-cost PIR can be acceptable when false negatives for still occupants are tolerable. For classroom people counting and persistent presence, mmWave radar is the more technically robust privacy-preserving class because it can detect fine motion that PIR often misses. If the goal is occupancy-aware environmental interpretation rather than precise counting, true CO2 plus schedule metadata and optional ML inference can be an economical secondary path, but it should be labeled clearly as inferred occupancy rather than direct measurement.
useful_output_and_units: Useful occupancy outputs are binary presence, estimated people count, occupancy density in persons per square meter or per room, occupancy duration in minutes, person-hours per day, and transition events such as class start, break, and vacancy recovery. These outputs become most valuable when aligned with CO2 ppm, temperature in degrees Celsius, relative humidity in percent, and time-above-threshold metrics for the occupied period.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: Camera, mmWave, ToF, and doorway counting provide explicit occupancy observations, although each still has edge cases and counting error. CO2, VOC, temperature, humidity, Wi-Fi association, and schedule data are occupancy proxies or inference inputs. They can be very useful operationally, but they should not be presented as direct occupancy measurements because ventilation, weather, and metabolic variation confound the relationship.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: PIR measures motion-linked changes in infrared radiation and is selective for movement rather than stable human presence. mmWave radar resolves range, motion, and fine micro-movements and can detect breathing-level motion that PIR misses. Camera-based systems are strongest for count and flow but raise the largest privacy burden. IAQ-based inference uses statistical or machine-learning relationships rather than a human-sensing physics principle, so its selectivity depends on the quality of labels and confounder handling.
useful_range_and_real_performance: Operationally, classroom occupancy sensing should handle empty rooms, partial occupancy, and full-capacity periods without saturating. The reviewed evidence shows that occupancy can be predicted from environmental data with up to 93% presence accuracy and 2.17 mean absolute error for exact count in the Slovenian elementary-school case, while the classroom edge-vision deployment by Monti et al. reported a maximum MAE of 1.23. Sulistiyanti et al. also reported occupancy-linked sensing accuracy of 97.17% for five-person scenarios and 93.96% for ten-person scenarios, alongside a CO2 correlation coefficient of 0.982 with student count.
operating_regime: Continuous operation during school hours is preferred. For direct sensing, event-level detection at seconds resolution can later be aggregated to 1 minute or 5 minute summaries. For control applications, pre-class, in-class, break, and post-class segments should be explicitly recognized because the meaning of the same CO2 or temperature value changes substantially across those regimes.
interferences_and_confounders: PIR misses still occupants and can be fooled by only transient motion. Cameras and doorway counters are affected by occlusion, backlighting, furniture layout, and people entering in groups. mmWave can be affected by placement, clutter, and complex reflections. IAQ-based occupancy inference is confounded by ventilation rate, window opening, weather, room volume, lesson type, and differences in metabolic and vocal activity.
affordable_validation_protocol: A practical TCC-scale protocol is to instrument one or two classrooms with the chosen occupancy sensor, collect manual head counts at 5 to 10 minute intervals during selected classes for at least 1 to 2 weeks, and log the timetable, window state, and break periods. If an IAQ-based inference model is tested, pair the labels with true CO2, temperature, humidity, and weather data, and reserve entire days or rooms for holdout testing. Short doorway video audits can be used temporarily as ground truth even when the final deployed system is camera-free.
validation_metrics: Minimum metrics are binary occupancy accuracy, precision, recall, false vacancy rate, MAE for people count, confusion at class transitions, uptime, and missing-data fraction. For IAQ-based inference, also report room-wise generalization, drift across seasons, and whether the model transfers to rooms with different volumes, schedules, and ventilation patterns.
installation_and_enclosure: Environmental nodes that support occupancy interpretation should remain in the breathing zone and away from direct drafts or solar gain. PIR needs a clear view of typical motion paths, while mmWave and ToF need a field of view that covers seated occupants rather than only door traffic. Camera or radar devices should avoid glare, dead angles, and direct obstruction by whiteboards, projectors, cabinets, or hanging fixtures.
hardware_integration: Occupancy sensing integrates well with ESP32-class MCUs for PIR and some radar modules, while edge-vision approaches usually require a Raspberry Pi class device or stronger accelerator. The most maintainable classroom architecture is often a combined environmental node plus a separate occupancy channel, because the data rates, privacy requirements, and failure modes differ substantially between them.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] Classroom occupancy cost varies strongly by sensing class. A coarse PIR-based occupancy channel can be added very cheaply at component level, whereas mmWave, ToF, or edge-vision nodes usually require materially higher sensor, compute, enclosure, and commissioning cost. In practice, classroom deployments tend to range from very low-cost presence sensing to mid-cost privacy-preserving counting, with camera-based systems often incurring the highest total governance and integration overhead rather than only hardware cost.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is moderate to high for the claim that occupancy and activity strongly shape classroom CO2 and comfort conditions. It is moderate for explicit classroom people counting and for IAQ-based occupancy inference, and lower for universal transferability across room types and institutions. The privacy literature is also maturing, especially where seemingly benign environmental streams can still reveal sensitive occupancy patterns.
variable_specific_cautions: Do not confuse occupancy presence with occupancy count, and do not confuse count with activity intensity. PIR is not a people counter. CO2-inferred occupancy lags and depends on ventilation. Device-based or schedule-based occupancy can be wrong in both directions. Even non-imaging environmental data can reveal sensitive behavior patterns, so privacy risk does not disappear simply because cameras are avoided.
system_architecture: A defensible architecture is room node plus occupancy stream plus gateway or campus network plus time-series storage plus dashboard. The occupancy layer can come from explicit sensing, schedule integration, or both. The highest-value outputs are not raw occupancy traces alone, but occupancy-normalized environmental indicators, class-transition events, and alerts that point facilities staff or teachers to concrete ventilation or room-management actions.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi with MQTT or HTTPS is the most straightforward for pilots. KNX/BAS integration is attractive when occupancy is expected to influence HVAC control directly. Edge devices that process occupancy locally and send only counts or states are preferable to transmitting raw images or high-volume radar data whenever privacy and bandwidth are concerns.
interoperability_and_data_model: The minimum data model should include timestamp, room ID, sensor ID, occupancy state or count, confidence or QA flag, and if available schedule state. To be operationally useful, occupancy records should also align cleanly with environmental variables, window or HVAC state, and lesson metadata such as course block or room use type.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Occupancy monitoring is significantly more sensitive than temperature or CO2 alone. The 2025 Slovenian study is especially important because it shows that occupancy can be inferred from environmental sensing, creating privacy implications even without cameras. Minimize retention of raw sensitive data, prefer edge processing, avoid personally identifiable analytics, define clear access roles, and ensure that classroom monitoring is framed as environmental and operational support rather than behavioral surveillance of teachers or students.
analytical_methods: Useful methods include descriptive time-series analysis by class period, correlation between occupancy and CO2, occupancy classification and regression, sensor fusion with schedules and weather, anomaly detection for overcapacity or prolonged stale air, and mixed objective-subjective analysis linking measured conditions to occupant feedback.
derived_index_or_model: Important derived measures are occupancy density, person-hours, occupied-period exceedance of IAQ thresholds, vacancy recovery time, and where appropriate inferred occupancy from environmental data. Inference models should state clearly whether they predict binary presence, coarse occupancy bands, or exact count, because these are different tasks with different error tolerance.
decision_rules_and_standards: There is no single classroom occupancy-sensing standard that resolves every deployment choice, so operational rules should be tied to use case. Practical rules include triggering pre-occupancy purge before scheduled classes, prioritizing rooms where measured or inferred occupancy repeatedly exceeds the ventilation assumptions used by the building, and treating unexplained high CO2 during supposedly low-occupancy periods as a prompt to inspect sensing, schedules, or ventilation operation.
intervention_and_automation: Occupancy-aware monitoring supports demand-responsive ventilation, pre-class flushing, post-class recovery, room reassignment for overcrowded groups, and better interpretation of alarms. It can also reduce false conclusions, for example distinguishing a ventilation problem from an unusually dense or highly vocal class session. Automation should remain transparent and should degrade safely if occupancy sensing fails.
environmental_outcomes: The main environmental gain is better attribution. Occupancy context makes CO2, temperature, and humidity trends interpretable, reduces false positives, and helps identify whether poor conditions arise from overcrowding, weak ventilation, or unusual activity. It also supports fairer comparison between classrooms with different schedules and densities.
health_and_learning_outcomes: Evidence is strongest for indirect benefit rather than a direct causal effect of occupancy sensing itself. When occupancy context is captured well, classrooms with repeated under-ventilation, overcrowding, or discomfort can be identified earlier, which supports cleaner air, reduced stuffiness, and better conditions for attention and learning. The KNX study also shows that subjective responses can diverge from sensor values, reinforcing the need to combine both.
objective_subjective_integration: A strong pattern across recent educational monitoring work is that subjective comfort and IAQ perceptions do not map perfectly onto one sensor stream. The Romanian KNX study explicitly combined sensor data with occupant feedback, showing why contextual interpretation should include both objective measurements and classroom-reported experience.
quantitative_results: Sulistiyanti et al. 2024 reported a correlation coefficient of 0.982 between student count and CO2 level, with occupancy-sensing accuracy of 97.17% for five-person scenarios and 93.96% for ten-person scenarios. Vake et al. 2025 reported up to 93% accuracy for occupancy presence and 2.17 MAE for exact people count inferred from IAQ and weather data in an elementary-school setting. Monti et al. 2022 reported a maximum MAE of 1.23 for classroom people counting with an edge-based camera approach. Rus et al. 2025 found strong alignment between fixed KNX and professional monitor data, with correlations up to 0.98 for CO2 and relative humidity and up to 0.97 for temperature, but also showed that subjective IAQ remained mixed despite acceptable tracking performance.
feasibility_and_acceptance: Occupancy/context sensing is feasible in classroom IoT systems, but the best sensing class depends on the question being asked. Acceptance is usually highest for privacy-preserving modalities and for dashboards that show aggregate room conditions rather than individual behavior. The biggest implementation risks are not only hardware cost, but governance, labeling effort, and the temptation to overinterpret proxies as precise counts.
validity_and_limitations: Ground truth is costly, room layouts differ, and models trained in one school may not transfer cleanly to another. Environmental inference can fail when ventilation changes faster than occupancy, and direct sensors can fail when occupants are still, clustered, or occluded. Results therefore need room-level validation, explicit statement of sensing limits, and caution before scaling from one building or institution to another.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature already supports a practical hierarchy for classroom context sensing: explicit privacy-preserving occupancy sensing where count matters, simpler presence sensing where it does not, and environmental inference only when labeled clearly as a proxy. The main gaps are standardized classroom benchmark datasets, better protocols for aligning occupancy with subjective and environmental data, stronger comparison of mmWave, ToF, PIR, and edge-vision under real classroom layouts, and clearer governance frameworks for privacy-preserving school deployment.
